welcome the Bill to amend the State Financial Corporations Act. Sir, this Bill was 
long overdue. In fact, we are discussing this Amendment to the State Financial 
Corporation Act, when the small and medium scale industries in the entire 
country are facing difficulties. 
The small and medium scale industries have played a very vital role in 
the Indian economy. The State Financial Corporations have also played a very 
dynamic role in promoting the small-scale industries in the country. 
But, Sir, today's scenario is quite different. The small-scale industries 
almost all over the country are facing difficulties. 
SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Figures di ffer. Some reports say nearly 
40-45 per cent of the small-scale industries are at the closure stage. In the case 
of some of them it may be because of administrative lapses or because of those 
people who have not been able to raise these industries properly. But, today, 
the small-scale industries are suffering mainly because of unequal competition 
and liberal imports. From 1992 onwards, the Government started thinking of 
various changes in the State Financial Corporations Act. Under section 4 of the 
Act, an effort is being made to expand the activities of the small-scale industries. 
It has now been suggested in the Bill to include several other activities like 
providing finances to management services, financial services, health services, 
software and hardware technology, telecommunications, providing commercial 
complex facilities and so on. While doing this, we have to be very careful. For 
example, take the construction industry. What type of construction activities 
should we include? Then there are similar other activities. While you define the 
industry, you have to consider the area of their activities as well. 
Financial Corporations are established to promote small-scale and 
medium-scale industries, which will simultaneously generate employment 
oppurtunities. There are certain activities included in Section 4 of the Act, which 
will not help in creation of employment opportunities. If a lot of finances go to 
such activities, they will not generate employment. We should be careful on this 
aspect. Small-scale industries have played a great role in creating employment 
opportunities as well as self-employment opportunities. 
Another important thing in this Bill is the question of raising capital. 
300 

[21 AUGUST, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
I welcome this, because the State Financial Corporations through this Bill are 
given power to raise capital. So far, the captial for the Financial Corporations 
was being contributed either through the State Governments or through the 
national financial institutions or through the IDBI. Now, SIDBI is being brought in 
as a monitoring agency, instead of IDBI. Earlier various other financial 
institutions used to contribute to the State Financial Corporations. 
Now, this Bill authorises the State Financial Corporations to raise 
capital, up to 49 per cent, from the market, in addition to from the State 
Government, other financial institutions and from the SIDBI. As a result, the 
State Financial Corporations will become more competitive. They will have to 
be made more accountable. The State Financial Corporations by going to the 
public for raising capital, are making themselves more accountable. This is the 
best thing. Up till now, they were not made strictly accountable because they 
were accountable to the Government or to some financial institution. But now 
they will be subjected to public scrutiny because public will be investing in their 
capital. This is also a welcome change. Then, I would like to seek one 
clarification from the hon. Minister. Now there is a provision in the Bill to reduce 
the capital. Section 4E states, "The Financial Corporation, with the prior 
approval of the State Government and the Small Industries Bank, may, by 
resolution passed in a general meeting of the shareholders, reduce its share 
capital in any way." When you are talking of increasing the share capital, .why 
should there be a provision for reducing the share capital? I would like to know 
from the hon. Minister as to why such a provision is there. 
Sir, while appreciating the various measures which have been 
brought in by the Government, I would like to point out that all is not well with the 
managements of the State Financial Corporations. We have seen that there is a 
lot of red-tapism in the State Financial Corporations. If a small-scale unit 
submits a proposal for sanctioning of a loan, the proposal may take one or two 
years. The proposals are not considered. Time is the essence in an industry. As 
a result of this, there is no transparency. We are living in an era of transparency. 
There should be accountability on the part of financial institutions or on the part 
of the State Financial Corporations to sanction loans before a certain time. A 
timeframe should be fixed. 
In fact, there are several articles published on the functioning of the 
301 

RAJYA SABHA [21 AUGUST, 2000] 
State Financial Corporations wherein it has been clearly stated that the State 
Financial Corporations should be able to give their consent for financing a 
project within a certain time; a time-limit should be fixed, say, 30 days or 40 days 
or 50 days. They can do it, possibly through a good and integrated data system. 
For instance, if a borrower approaches a State Financial Corporation for setting 
up an industry, for a specific project with a specific installed capacity and 
location of a project, the SFC should be in a position to say, by having a proper 
data, that they are going to sanction the loan by such and such time. Now, there 
is a lot of red-tapism. Regarding the sanctioning of loans, I would not like to go 
into the details. My point is transparency has to be brought in while processing a 
loan application and in sanctioning of it. 
Another important thing which has probably escaped attention is 
section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act wherein they have been given 
the power to take over a unit if it defaults in payment. When you recover the 
loan, you have to be firm in recovering the loan. We agree with that. Now, 
section 29 gives a power to the State Financial Corporation to take over a unit if 
it defaults in payment. Under section 29, a number of instances are there where 
a running unit has been taken over because of default in payment and the unit 
will suffer and will be almost killed. They will not take action immediately. When 
the unit is taken, if you want to sell it, you will not realise anything. You will have 
to sell it at a throw-away price. Sometimes, they take over a unit, lock it and keep 
it for one year. The unit will lose its value. Its market is lost. I am not saying, for a 
moment, that you should dilute the powers of the State Financial Corporation as 
far as the recovery measures are concerned. In fact, this matter has been dealt 
with by the Supreme Court also. The Supreme Court has given certain 
guidelines as to the use of section 29, what should be the various constraints. 
interruption). Constraint is there on me also. However, I would like to bring them 
to the notice of the hon. Minister. You should consider bringing certain 
amendments to the use of section 29. Even some articles have called it a 
draconian law. The Supreme Court, in Mahesh Chandra v. Regional Manager, 
UPFC, has formulated certain guidelines as to how it should be included. There 
is a complaint that while dealing with recovery under section 29, because of the 
misuse of section 29, industries have suffered. I would like to request the hon. 
Minister to look into this issue. 
Then, there is a need for a comprehensive law. These amendments

passed the Bill and the Bill is a progressive Bill. But there is a need for a

I once again welcome this Bill and I hope the hon. Minister will

Nitrates and Flouride in Ground Water of Delhi 
*408.  SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: SHRI 
SANJAY NIRUPAM: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that TERI has repo rted that the ground water in Delhi 
contains dangerously high quantities of Nitrates and Flouride which is harmful to 
health; and 
 if so, what action Government are taking to protect the people from this 
hazard? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN SETHI): (a) and (b) The 
Tata Energy and Research Institute (TERI) have not reported that "ground water in 
Delhi contains dangerously high quantities of nitrate and flouride which is harmful to 
health". However, a joint study made by the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) 
and the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) have reported the presence of high 
quantities of flouride and nitrate in ground water of some parts of Alipur, Kanjhawala, 
Najafgarh, Shahdara and city blocks of Delhi. 
Water being a State subject, provision of drinking water supply is the responsibility 
of the State Governments. The Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission has 
however been assisting and guiding the States in providing safe drinking water to rural 
areas under the Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme and exclusive sub-
mission programmes in areas having serious ground wa ter quality problems like 
flouride, iron arsenic and brackishness. In su ch areas where ground water is unfit for 
drinking, safe drinking water is provided through alternative sources, either by tapping 
surface water or by undertaking remedial measures like deflouridation, iron and 
arsenic removal. A total of 632 defluoridation plants, 150 desalination plants and 9524 
iron removal plants have been installed at different places in various States. 
The steps taken by the Union Government and the Delhi Jal Board to protect the 
people from this hazard include: 
(i) The Delhi Jal Board produces about 640 Million Gallon/Day (MGD) water. Out 
of this 72 MGD (11.25%) is ground water 
32 

[22 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
and the remaining 568 MGD (88.75%) is surface water. The surface water is treated 
in modern treatment plants. Out of 72 MDG ground water, 6 MGD water is treated at 
an ozonisation and nitrification plant at Okhla in South Delhi and the rest is supplied 
after chlorination. 
(ii) Works of rain water harvesting/recharging of aquifer have been taken up by the 
Delhi Jal Board individually and also through the Resident Welfare 
Associations under Bhagidari Scheme. The Delhi Jal Board has taken up 65 
such projects. 
(iii) The project of prevention and control of fluorosis has been  launched by the 
Delhi Government's Health Department. 
(iv) A 40 MDG water treatment plant has recently been commissioned at Nangloi 
and a 20 MDG plant is nearing completion at Bawana. These plants shall 
draw raw water from surface sources only for treatment. 
(v) The Central Ground Water Authority has declared Najafgarh and Mehrauli 
blocks of Delhi as notified areas for control and regulated development of 
ground water. 
(vi) The Delhi Jal Board has identified hand pumps and other structures in polluted 
areas where the shallow ground water is not fit for human consumption and 
painted them red with warning. 
(vii) The Central Ground Water Authority has organised mass awareness 
programmes among the public, indus trialists and industrial workers 
regarding pollution and over-extraction of ground water. 
(viii) The Central Ground Water Board is periodically monitoring water quality for 
the NCT Delhi.

 whether Government propose to withdraw the surcharge on income tax as

amount of income-tax paid every month by Government Officials of any particular 
cadre.

specified savings, and taking into account other deductions and exemptions, the

10(15) of the Income-tax Act.

reviews saving schemes provided for priority sectors during the 
annual budget exercise. Some of the steps taken to provide short and 
long term savings in priority sectors, include tax rebate under 
Section-88 for investments in equity shares or bonds made by a public 
company developing infrastructure facility. Under Section 54EC, long

new law (the Competition Act).

Authority (to be known as the Competition Commission of India) to look into and

mergers/ amalgamations that might lead to abuse of dominance and agreements

Practices Act, 1969 and winding up of the MRTP Commission.

rivers were referred to the tribunals under Inter State Water Disputes Act, 1956 in 
1969. The Tribunals have submitted the final report to Central Government in 1980,

from the Tribunal under Section 5(3) of the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956.

relief to State of Tamil Nadu and Union Territory of Pondicherry. The Central 
Government has published the interim order in the official gazette on 10.12.91 making 
it final and binding on the parties to the disputes. In pursuance of order of the 
Supreme Court dated 9.4.1997, the Central Government has framed a scheme under 
Section 6A of the said Act for giving effect to the interim order and all its related 
subsequent orders. The scheme consists of the Cauvery River Authority headed by the 
Prime Minister with the Chief Ministers of the basin States as its members. The 
Authority is assisted by a Monitoring Committee headed by the Secretary (Water 
Resources).

India has been fighting efforts to patent inherently traditional items like 
neem, karela, basmati, etc. Now, it seems th at the spiritual heritage of meditation like 
Kundalini, Nataraj, Nadabrahma, etc. have all been applied for trademark in the USA.

cassettes, paintings of Acharya Rajneesh, along with meditational techniques, have 
been applied for. There is a danger of losing these assets of the civilisation of India.

DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY (Nominated) : Mr. Chairman, Sir, I seek your 
kind permission to make a Special Mention on the harm to the students caused by fake 
universities. More than ever, today the youth are career-conscious. They plan their

very important for the students. During this period, they will be entering the 
universities. In India, we are facing the menace of fake universities. In reply to my

universities. The youth in thei r anxiety to get admission into universities may fall a 
prey to fake universities. I feel that more effective steps are needed now. The 
Malpractice Prevention Cells in educational in stitutions should be strengthened in all 
respects. Mere press releases by the University Grants Commission are not sufficient. 
Publicity on fake universities should be carried out on a massive scale in the 
newspapers and electronic media. Sir, very st ringent measures are needed to arrest the 
mischief of fake universities. I appeal to the Government to take immediate measures 
in the matter, otherwise the career of many students will be affected.   Thank you.

Government and the House to the procedure of releasing funds from the Prime

meet the expenses of treatment. So, there is a genuine need for increasing the amount. 
I earnestly request the hon. Prime Minister to take appropriate steps on the 
above matters so as to enhance the utility of the scheme.

Rs.80,000 in the case of death and Rs.90,000 in the case of permanent disablement, 
the amounts should be further increased to a minimum of Rs.One lakh and 
Rs.1,25,000 respectively. Disablement may occur at a young age and the man has to 
live all his life in disablement and suffer. Therefore, the rates must be increased. Also, 
in view of the fact that for about 40 years, these smaller amounts had been provided in 
the previous

enactment, and we do not know when again we shall consider further amendments to 
the Schedule, depending upon the exigencies of the situation, the present rates should 
go up. Therefore, I suggest Rs.One lakh for death and Rs. 1,25,000 for permanent 
disablement. 
I would also suggest that insurance should be compulsorily provided. In the 
absence of insurance, a lot of problems arise in the matter of getting the compensation

The other provision which, I suggest, should be amended is this. It has been

I stand to support the Bill. The Bill makes two small amendments which are 
for the benefit of the workmen. Therefore, they are welcome. Employment of a casual 
nature is now covered. And there is a marginal increase in the pecuniary limit. So far, 
so good. Therefore, I compliment the hon. Minister for bringing this measure. But I 
believe that much remains to be done in th is behalf. Strangely, while including those 
persons whose employment is of a casual nature and who are employed otherwise 
than for purposes of the employer's trade or business, Schedule II of the Act excludes 
those who are working in a clerical capacity. In fact, if casual employment is also 
covered by the Act, it is all the more necessary that the employment of those who are 
working in a clerical capacity should also be covered. The crux of the matter, insofar 
as workmen's compensation is concerned, is the injury which arises out of and during 
the course of employment. And a clerk, as every other worker, is in the place where he 
meets with the accident because of his employment. The age-old test laid down by 
Justice Chagte is, "Why was he there? He was there only because of his employment. 
And therefore, he is entitled to compensation." That equally applies to clerks, and 
therefore, they should also be covered by this

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2000] 
benefit of compensation. I may mention that in a comparable enactment, namely, the 
ESI Act, clerks are covered, and there is no reason why they are not covered by the 
Workmen's Compensation Act. I have another suggestion to make in so far as the 
amount of compensation that is made payable is concerned. The computation of the 
compensation under section 4, read with Schedule 4, is done in a manner which is not 
intelligible to common man, maybe, sometimes, to the lawyers, because an acturial 
method is employed and a smaller figure is ultimately computed even though the 
workman is getting a salary of a proportionately higher range. So, the increase of the 
limit to Rs. 4,000/- is, as a matter of fact, ridiculous, looking to the value of the rupee 
which it has attained during the last few year s, and therefore, it will be reasonable if 
the compensation is based on the emoluments of the employee, without depending 
upon the higher limit, and whatever the emoluments, the compensation should be 
commensurate to those emoluments. I have mentioned already that the aspect of 
computation is unintelligible, and that so metimes brings injustice to the workman 
concerned. 
There is a third aspect to which I would like to draw the attention both of the 
House and the Minister, and it is regarding the list of occupational diseases in the 
enactment. This list today is thoroughly outdated, particularly in view of the fact that 
the increase in the industries with chemicals is enormous, and in fact, because of 
several international conventions, the Factories Act has been amended to introduce a 
substantial chapter to cover hazardous substances and safety measures in so far as the 
workmen are concerned. In fact, the rules under the Act make it mandatory for the 
employer to subject his employees to medical examination every six months. The 
diseases that one gets afflicted with because of his exposure to various hazardous 
substances and chemicals, are not covered by the Act, because the diseases which 
were considered occupational almost a century ago, even though the enactment is of 
1923, are only the diseases covered by the enactment. Therefore, the Schedule in 
respect of occupational diseases which is thoroughly outdated, ought to be replaced, to 
include diseases for which protection is sought by express provisions under the 
Factories Act. 
Lastly, I would submit that the definition of compensation should also be 
reviewed. Today, an employee is entitled to compensation as provided by an 
enactment. But we have industries where trade unions are strong and they enter into 
agreements providing for higher compensation.

That provision in the agreement is given a go-by, taking recourse to a statutory limit, 
and the employer says, even though it is agreed, the statute says that he will not get 
that. Therefore, the definition of compensation which is now only that which is 
governed by the Act, must also include compensation, as is agreed between the 
parties, naturally whichever is higher. I, therefore, submit that even though this Bill is 
meant for the benefit of the employees, it does its job only marginally in so far as the 
diseases covered, in so far as the employees , including clerks covered are concerned.   
With this, I support the Bill. Thank you.

Madam Deputy Chairperson, the Workmen's Compensation (Amendment) 
Bill needs a thorough and detailed revision. The reasons for demanding  such  a 
revision are  many.     Take,  for example,  the  list  of 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [22 August, 2000] 
occupational diseases, which is given in the Schedule of the Act. The Member who 
spoke earlier has stated that it is almost outmoded. When newer and newer industries 
have come into being, new methods of production, new methods of operation, new 
products are being introduced. Several types of energy are being used. Several types of 
equipment are being employed in industry and trade. Several diseases-heart problems, 
bone-related diseases, damages to eyes and brain, skin diseases-are reported to be 
connected with occupational hazards. The list of occupational hazards does not 
consider these diseases; that list is outmoded outright. These things should be 
examined thoroughly, and an amendment to the Act should be brought in. That is point 
number one I want to say. 
The minimum amount of compensation has been increased. It is welcome. 
But it is inadequate. In the case of fatal accidents, for permanent disablement, an 
amount of Rs.90,000/- is being fixed as compensation. It is totally inadequate. It 
should be a minimum of Rs.1.5 lakhs. Not only that; for permanent total disablement, 
a worker who is affected by an accident should be given pension till his death. Not 
only that; the next of kin or dependent should be given employment in the industry 
where the employee works and meets with an accident. 
The expenditure for funeral has also been increased. But nowadays, the 
amount, taking into consideration the expenses of funeral, should be enhanced to at 
least Rs. 10,000/-. 
There is a very good suggestion to include casual and temporary workers to 
be benefited by the Workmen's Compensation Act. It is welcome. But I demand that 
every worker, whether he is a clerk or a supervisor or a manager, should be covered 
by the Act, and the benefit should be awarded to him. 
The third point which I want to stress is that in factories and industrial 
establishments, the precaution taken for prevention of accidents is totally inadequate. 
The Factories Act and many other labour laws have some provisions regarding the 
safety of workers, but the managements gi ve only low priority to those rules and 
regulations. It should be thoroughly examined, and a proper legislation should be 
brought. That is my third point. 
244 

[22 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Lastly, I would like to stress that the workers, who are handling these 
products and machines and transporting these goods, should be given training on how 
to deal with them. Many poisonous, inflammable, explosive and dangerous substances 
are transported by rail, road and other modes of transport. Many accidents are taking 
place. Not only the workers but the general public also are affected by these accidents. 
How do we deal with the situation? The workers should be thoroughly trained in 
dealing with these things. Proper instructions should be displayed on the vehicles that 
carry such explosive substances. This type of amendments should be made to the 
Workmen's Compensation Act. Then only can the accidents be prevented. Measures 
capable of preventing accidents should be taken and implemented properly. 
While supporting the Bill, I request the hon. Minister to come forward with 
a comprehensive amendment to the Workmen's Compensation Act. Thank you.

SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA (KARNA TAKA): Sir, the hon. Finance 
Minister has come with Appropriation (No. 3) Bill, 2000 and Appropriattion (No. 4) 
Bill, 2000, seeking appropriation of certain amounts. Rs.2536.66 crores have spent not 
on the productive lines. Whatever the reasons for asking for appropriation of money 
are, the funds given in the Budget are not utilised for generation of income. Amounts 
are now required to be utilised for meeting expenses on salaries and spending on 
unproductive lines. 
I want to point out to the hon. Finance Minister that after Pokhran, 
the developed countries imposed sanctions against us. There was a fear 
that Indian economy would be destabilised, but because of agriculture, there 
were  no  far-reaching  effects  on  Indian  economy. After  the  WTO 
agreement, see what the fate of agriculturists in this country is. Due to import of 
various agricultural products, the farmer is suffering badly. He is not getting just and 
reasonable prices for his products like v paddy, potato, coconut, jute, tobacco, coffee, 
tea, cardamom sugar, for anything. Apart from that, there is no lifting of sugar; so the 
grower of sugarcane is feeling very bad. Sugar mills are not paying sufficient prices. 
Whom should we blame? Under such circumstances, I would like to draw the attention 
of the Finance Minister to the fact that it is only due to globalisation that the prices are 
going down. I would like to know from the Finance Minister that if it is a fact, why the 
prices of fertilizers are not coming down. They are increasing day by day. I would like 
to bring to the notice of the Finance Minister that in 1998 we requested him in this 
House to reduce the price of urea. It was enhanced by one rupee per kilo. He said, "It 
is too difficult and we will ro ll back 50 paise". You co mpare the prices now. The 
prices of fertilizers, tractor, diesel and all agricultural inputs are going up day by day. 
The prices of agricultural products are coming down. How do you maintain an 
equilibrium? How are you goin g to balance it? Now, we are experiencing a white 
revolution throughout the country. It was done, firstly by Gujarat, secondly by 
Karnataka, and thirdly by Andhra Pradesh, and so on. You are importing a lot of milk 
and milk products at the cost of the poor agriculturists. Apart from that, I would like to 
draw the attention of the Finance Minister to the fact that 70 per cent of the Indian 
families, who are dependent on agricutlure, are getting their major income by selling

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA); Sir, I am 
extremely grateful to some 13 hon. Memb ers—thirteen is incidentally our lucky 
number-of this House, starting with Mr. S.B. Chavan and ending with Mr. Javare 
Gowda, who have participated in this discussion and made a number of very valuable 
suggestions. Mr. Chavan started by raising the issue of globalisation and 
liberalisation. This is the theme which has been reiterated by a number of hon. 
Members of this House.   Sir, when we took

office in March, 1998, in our first incarnation, we did not get a clean slate to write 
upon. There was a tot which was already written on that slate. There were 
international obligations, international treaty obligations which had to be honoured. 
Governments come and go. But many of the obligations, especially international 
obligations continue to subsist. The most potent instrument of globalisation or of the 
new form of globalisation is supposed to be the WTO. I was a Member of this House 
in those days. I remember a number of occasions when along with other colleagues in 
this House I raised issues regarding the Uruguay Round of .Negotiations. Before the 
Dunkel proposals, the name that we knew was the Uruguay Round of Negotiations. 
Then the Dunkel proposals came. The Dunke l proposals were so dangerous that I 
remember, out of sheer agitation, I travelled 250 kilometres on a bicycle with some 
200 friends of mine from the BJP to which I belong. We stopped at every village, 
every market place and every town on the way and told the people about the danger of 
the proposals formulated by Mr. Dunkel. But the new WTO Treaty was signed in 
Marrakesh. We assumed those obligations. Today we have been accused of removing 
quantitative restrictions. We have been accused of opening up the economy of the 
country for imports from other countries. Sir, a reference has been made to 714 items 
from which quantitative restrictions have been removed this year. Sir, I would like to 
say that neither .the Government of the day nor the trade and industry of this country 
went into the details of the obligations that  we were assuming. Nobody really studied 
as to what the impli cations of the WTO Treaty would be. Today we are left with that 
obligation. I would like to mention how we are trying to tackle it. So far as the 
removal of quantitative restrictions is concerned, it is not a sin which has been 
committed by this Government for the firs t time. Before 1.4. 1996, quantitative 
restrictions were removed from 6161 items. In 1996-97, quantitative restrictions were 
removed from 488 items. In 1997-98, agai n quantitative restrictions were- removed 
from 391 items. In 1998-99, quantitative restrictions were removed from 894 items. In 
1999-2000, quantitative restrictions have been removed from 714 items. Out of 10,202 
items, there are still 715 items from which quantitative restrictions have to be removed 
by 1st April, 2001 in accordance with the treaty obligations which exist under the 
WTO. That is what it is. At the same time, while we are removing the quantitative 
restrictions, it is not that we are completely unmindful or ignorant of the impact that it 
might have on the Indian industry, especially the small-scale industry and the Indian 
agriculture. Let me hasten to add that because we are aware of this problem and    
because it is a

policy of the Government that we shall protect both the Indian industry and the Indian 
agriculture; that we shall protect the interests of the Indian economy, we have already 
taken a number of steps in order to be able to do so. Sir, I would like to take the House 
into confidence -- though this is something which I have included in my Budget and is 
well known -- and say that customs duty on all agricultural, horticultural and dairy 
produce, was taken to the peak rate of 35% in this year's Budget, across- the-board. 
All agricultural products have been now charged of duty at the peak rate. All items, in 
respect of which QRs were removed in April this year, have also been taken to the 
peak rates. In the case of sugar, wheat, rice, edible oils, the tariff rate was fixed at 
100% to enable adjustments in rates during the current year and we have already 
raised the rates wherever it was necessary. Basic customs duty on chicken meat and 
chicken products was increased to 100% with effect from 12.5.2000. Similarly, basic 
customs duty on tea and coffee was increased from 15% to the peak rate of 35% with 
effect from 12.5.2000. Basic customs duty on crude as well as refined edible oils was 
increased on 12.6.2000. Basic customs duty on powdered milk and corn was increased 
from nil to 60% on 12.6.2000. Basic customs duty on arecanut was increased from 
35% to 100% on 6.7.2000. So, wherever we have the manoeuvrability, in terms of the 
WTO-bound rates, we are using that in orde r to protect our agriculture and industry. 
And this will continue to be the policy of this Government. 
Sir, there is fair competition and there is unfair competition. Unfair 
competition takes place when goods are dumped into this country. I would like to take 
the House into confidence and say that despite a somewhat laborious process that we 
have, in this country, of imposing anti-dumping duties, we have so far imposed anti-
dumping duties in about 105 cases; not one, two or thirty, but in 105 cases we have 
imposed anti-dumping duties. At present, there are 40 items on which this is valid. In 
addition, safeguard duty is presently applicable on three items against which we had 
received representations. So, Sir, it cannot be said that we have been found wanting, in 
terms of action, as far as protecting the do mestic industry and domestic agriculture is 
concerned. And I would like to once again reiterate that whenever we receive a 
complaint that any sector of our industry or any sector of our agriculture is being 
affected adversely by imports, we will be taki ng this step. But, Sir, let me also inform 
the House that as far as agricultural imports are concerned, I have got the figures of 
1998-99 and 1999-2000;  and the figures speak for themselves;  despite what  Nilotpal

Now, I come to the second important issue which has been raised by a 
number of our colleagues, cutting across party lines, in this House, and that is the issue 
of the 11th Finance Commission. Sir, we are all aware that the Finance Commission is 
constituted every five years under the provisions of the Indian Constitution. The 
framers of the Constitution decided that there must be an independent body which 
will, every five years, decide on the very  sensitive issue of devolution of Central 
funds, Central taxes, to the States, and the distribution, the horizontal distribution, of 
that devolution among the States. So, basically, what the Finance Commission decides 
is in regard to how much of the Central taxes should be devolved to the States and 
how the moneys thus available should be distributed among the various States. Now, a 
debate has been started in this country in regard to the recommendations of the 
Finance Commission. A point of view has been mentioned here, Sir, that we should 
have discussed the matter with the State Governments before we came to a conclusion, 
and before we submitted the Action Taken Report to Parliament. Sir, I will most 
humbly submit that with regard to the Report of the 10th

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN : Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing 
away of Shri P.R. Kumaramangalam, Minister of Power, on the 23rd August, 2000 at 
the young age of 48. 
Born in May, 1952, at Madras, Shri Kumaramangalam had his education at 
Madras University and then got a degree in Law from Delhi University. An active 
student union leader, he was the founder-Presi dent of the N.S.U.I. Subsequently, Shri 
Kumaramangalam was associated with various trade union activities and carved out a 
niche for himself in the trade union movement  in India, with his sharp intellect, 
outstanding negotiating skills and his devotion to the cause. 
"Ranga", as he was popularly know n, had a long and distinguished 
Parliamentary career. He was a Member of the Eighth, Ninth, Tenth, Twelfth and 
Thirteenth Lok Sabhas. He served as a Union Minister for several years and held the 
portfolios of Parliamentary Affairs, Law, Justice and Company Affairs, Science and 
Technology, Electronics, Ocean Developmen t and Power. During his Parliamentary 
career, his grasp of policy, his ability to marshal facts and his formidable debating skills 
were as impressive, as hi s great sense of humour, affability and openness was 
endearing. 
In the untimely passing away of Shri P.R. Kumaramangalam, the country has lost 
an eminent Parliamentarian, an outstanding administrator, a dynamic personality and a 
great crusader for the common man's cause. To me personally, and to all of us, his 
passing away is a great loss and he leaves behind a void, which we will all feel for a 
long time. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect 
to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute) 1 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2000] 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the bereaved family 
our sense of profound sorrow and deep sympathy. 
As a mark of respect to the memory of Shri RR. Kumaramangalam, the House stands 
adjourned till 11.00 a.m. on Friday, the 25th August, 2000.

OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing 
away of Shri Narayanrao Krishnarao Shejwalkar, a former Member of this House on the 
23rd August, 2000 at the age of seventy-seven. 
Born at Gwalior in August, 1923, Shri Shejwalkar had his education at Gwalior 
and Agra. An Advocate by profession, Shri Shejwalkar was a member of the Civil 
Liberties Union and the M.B. Education Society, Gwalior. He was a member of the 
Municipal Corporation of Gwalior for eight years and was its Mayor in 1960, 1969 and 
1970. Shri Shejwalkar was also associated  with various social welfare and cultural 
organisations. 
Shri Shejwalkar represented the State of Madhya Pradesh in Rajya Sabha from 
April 1968 to April 1974. Shri Shejwalkar was also a Member of the Sixth and the 
Seventh Lok Sabhas. 
In the passing away of Shri Shejwalkar, the country has lost a noted social 
worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Shejwalkar. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of respect 
to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI

service conditions, launching of Early Faculty Induction Programme to attract young 
talents to the teaching profession; and operation of various faculty development 
programmes like, quality improvement programmes, continuing education

     Protection of water resources from industrial pollution 
†443. SHRI VUAY SINGH YADAV: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 whether Government propose to protect the water resources from industrial 
pollution; 
 if so, the details thereof; 
 whether Government have made an assessment of the quantum of water 
being rendered unfit to use every year due to industrial pollution; and 
 if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was 
enacted with the objective of protecting water resources from pollution. Under this Act, 
a State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) in every State and Pollution Control Committee 
(PCC) in every Union Territory and the Central Pollution Control Board for the entire 
country have been set up. Industrial units discharging effluents are required to take 
consent from the SPCB/PCC, and thereafter the consent has to be renewed 
periodically. 
(c) and (d) The CPCB have estimated the waste water generated from different 
categories of industries to be 83,140 million litres per day (mid), including 73,975 mid 
from thermal power plants. The industrial effluent, if treated appropriately, can be 
used fully or partially for specific purposes.

SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH: 
Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that an experiment production of transgenic cotton was

 if so, the names of institutes which carried out such experiment and the

 whether agro-scientists had conducted any study about the post-experiment

(d) if so, the names of these scien tists and the details of their study

THE MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): 
(a) to (d) Contained limited field experiments on transgenic cotton were carried 
out in various regions of the country. These experiments were not for production of 
transgenic cotton but were for evaluation of transgenic characters in cotton plants i. e. the 
effect of an introduced transgene that codes for a protein (Bt protein), produced by 
Bacillus thuringiensis, a bacterium commonly  
†Original  notice of the question  was  received  in  Hindi. 
28 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
occurring in nature. During 1998-2000, evaluation of agronomic performance and on-
farm trials for transgenic cotton to ascertain the yield, morphological characteristics, 
persistence, germination rate and pest load were carried out by the scientists of M/s 
Maharashtra Hybrid Seeds Co. Ltd. (MAHYCO), Mumbai in private lands and State 
Agricultural Universities in the State of Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, 
Madhya Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu. The institutes were 
Acharya NG Ranga Agricultural University Rajendra Nagar, at its Regional Research 
Station, Lamb, Guntur, as well as at Warangal in Andhra Pradesh, Punjab Rao Krishi 
Vidyapeeth at Akola; and Marathwada Agricultural University, Parbhani in Maharashtra. 
The effect of Bt cottonseeds on goats as m odel was studied at the Indian Toxicological 
Research Centre (ITRC), Lucknow and Bt protein was not found to be toxic. The agro-
scientists of MAHYCO has conducted detailed post-harvest observations on the impact 
of Bt cotton cultivators at Ja lna in Maharashtra; Dharwad in Karnataka; Hyderabad in 
Andhra Pradesh and Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu. A team of over 20 scientists of R & D 
laboratory of MAHYCO led by Dr. Usha Zehr, Dr. S.K. Mukherjee and others 
conducted these experiments. It was concluded from these studies that there was 
significant increase in the yield from transgenic plants. There was also noticeable 
reduction in the spraying of chemical pesticides for bollworms, a major pest of cotton. 
The residues of Bt protein in soil were either non-existent or were extremely low and did 
not have any effect on the microbial popu lations of the soil samples. The Genetic 
Engineering Approval Committee has approved on 30lh June 2000, large scale field 
trials with scientific monitoring in some States. Work has started in the States of 
Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

*456. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
 whether the Supreme Court has asked the Centre to submit report on death of 
twelve tigers in the Nandankanan Zoo in Orissa, recently; and 
 if so, the details of the probe report submitted and the action taken based on 
that report? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Hon'ble Supreme Court directed the Ministry of Environment 
and Forests to place on record the report of the Committee which was appointed by the 
Ministry of Environment and Forests for inquiring into the death of tigers in 
Nandankanan Zoo and information as to the action taken thereupon. The Ministry of 
Environment and Forests has submitted a factual report to Hon'ble Supreme Court in 
this regard. The main recommendations of the report submitted by the Committee are as 
follows:— 
(i) Screening of tigers, lions and other animals should be conducted on a 
regular basis and appropriate treatment be provided on the basis of the 
screening results. 
(ii) Restraining facilities and isolation wards should be upgraded for 
effective treatment of the animals. 
(iii) Immediate repair of the safari and boundary wall to safeguard against 
ingress of livestock. 
(iv) All carnivores should be provided feed in individual feeding cells to 
ensure supply of food in hygien ic conditions and facilitating the 
physical handling of animals. 
(v)   Proper checking of the meat fed to the animals. 
(vi)   Improved cleanliness and better drainage. 
(vii) Officer of the level of at least Deputy Conservator of Forests should be 
stationed at part with adequate administrative and financial powers. 
(viii) Coordination between the Zoo Hospital and Orissa Veterinary College 
in matters of treatment of Zoo animals. 
On the basis of the above observations an d detailed consultations held with the 
State Government the following course of action has been agreed upon: 
48 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
 State Government would take necessary disciplinary action against the 
officials who were found lax in discharge of their duties. 
 Immediate action for reducing the overcrowding and providing each 
tiger/lion an individual feeding cells. 
 Periodic determination of parasitic loads in all the animals would be carried 
out and prophylactics would be provided wherever necessary. 
 The boundary wall of zoo and broken fencing of the Safari would be restored 
within three months. 
 Restraint facilities and the isolation wards attached to the zoo hospital would 
be upgraded immediately. 
(0 System for regular checking of the quality of meat and drinking water for the 
animals would be in place. 
(g) the hygiene and sanitation of the zoo shall be improved. 
(h) A panel of veterinarians and experts would be constituted for monitoring 
the implementation of the above recommendations. 
(i) State Government would permit direct flow of funds from the Central Zoo 
Authority to the zoo to avoid delay in execution of work of essential nature.

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) Ministry of Environment and Forests have received the report of 
the Committee which was constituted to ascertain the causes of deaths of tigers and to 
suggest ways to avoid recurrence of the same in Nandankanan Zoo, Orissa. The report 
has confirmed that the main cause of the death of tigers was 'Trypanosomiasis'. It has 
confirmed that the choice of the drug 'Berenil' used by the Zoo Administration was 
appropriate. It has also been observed that a large number of tigers in the zoo, lack of 
proper hygiene, and the onset of monsoon caused the increase in the incidence of 
vectors. The main recommendations of the report submitted by the Committee are as as 
follows:— 
(i) Screening of tigers, lions and other animals should be conducted on a 
regular basis and appropriate treatment be provided on the basis of the 
screening results. 
(ii) Restraining facilities and isolat ion wards should be upgraded for 
effective treatment of the animals. 
(iii) Immediate repair of the safari an d boundary wall to safeguard against 
ingress of livestock. 
(iv) All carnivores should be provided feed in individual feeding cells to 
ensure supply of food in hygienic conditions and facilitating the 
physical handling of animals. 
(v)   Proper checking of the meat fed to the animals. 
(vi)   Improved cleanliness and better drainage. 
(vii) Officer of the level of at least Deputy Conservator of Forests should be 
stationed at part with adequate administrative and financial powers.

in matters of treatment of zoo animals.

3417. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that fertilizer availability is a major factor for agricultural 
production, particularly foodgrains production;

FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAMESH BAIS): (a) and (b) Among seven inputs of 
agricultural production namely seeds, fertili zers, insecticides, pesticides, agricultural 
implements and machinery, water and technology and its transfer to farmers, fertilizers 
are one of the important inputs. No study quantifying the role of individual input has 
been made. The nutritional requirements of plants can be met by use of both organic 
and inorganic fertilizers, but availability of 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
right type of fertilizers on time and in adequate quantity have an important role.

Industry can not be categorized as a strategic industry. 
Based on the recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission, Government 
have decided to disinvest 51 % of its equity in National Fertilizers Limited (NFL) out of 
its current holding of 97.65% and 32.74% of its equity in Madras Fertilizers Limited

companies, namely The Fertilizer and Chemicals Travancore Limited (FACT), Pyrites,

disinvestment, the decision in the case of FACT and RCF has been deferred, whereas

companies namely, The Fertilizer Corporation of India Limited (FCI) and Hindustan 
Fertilizer Corporation Limited (HFC) have since been declared sick and therefore there

3418. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
 whether, in order to offset the loss to  the domestic industry, consequent on

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAMESH BAIS): (a) to (c) Urea is the only fertilizer which is 
under price, movement and distribution control and whose imports are made on 
Government account. The Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) on urea have to be lifted w.e.f. 
1.4.2001. The freeing of QRs, including those on urea, is a commitment India has 
entered into in an Agreement with USA in December, 1999 following the ruling of the 
Dispute Settlement Body of the WTO that 
58 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
India's QRs were not justified on balance of payments grounds. The Government has set 
up a Task Force to study the impact of removal of QRs on urea and suggest measures 
including that of bound rate which will be made applicable to protect the indigenous 
industry. The recommendations of the Tasks Force will form the basis for imposition 
of applied rate of tariff on urea imports. 
All other major fertilizers are decontrolled and their imports are being freely 
made on private trade account. Currently, tariff on Di-Ammonium Phosphate (DAP) 
and Sulphate of Potash (SOP) is 5% while it is 5.5% in respect of other fertilizers.

Essential Commodities Act In respect of decontrolled fertilizers, the Government has been fixing 
MRP under the Concession Scheme which is administered by the Department of Agriculture 
and Cooperation. So long as this arrangement continues, levying of tariff may have no 
impact on the market prices.

Ganga Action Plan 
3429. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
 what is the present stage of Ganga Action Plan; 
 to what extent Ganga has been purified; and 
 at the present rate, how long it will take to complete the Ganga Action Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) The Ganga Action Plan has been taken up in 
two phases. Under the first phase started in June 1985 at a cost of Rs. 462.04 crore, an 
amount of Rs. 451.70 crore has been utilised by the Go vernment of India. In addition 
an amount of Rs. 477.25 crore has been utilised so far out of allocated funds of Rs. 
1276.26 crore on the second phase of the Ganga Action Plan approved in stages 
between 1993 to 1996. 
(b) The target fixed for the implementation of the Ganga Action Plan Phase I 
was to bring the water quality of the river Ganga to the "bathing class" standards which 
is as under:  
Bio-chemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) 3 mg/1 (maximum) 
Dissolved Oxygen (DO) 5 mg/1 (minimum) 
Total Coliform (MPN) 10,000 per 100 ml 
Fecal Coliform (MPN) 2,500 per 100 ml 
The present level of Bio-chemical oxygen demand, an indicator of pollution is 
lower than the level in 1986, The range of Bio-chemcial oxygen demand level which 
was 1.7 to 15.5 in 1986 has come down to 1.0 to 6.5 in 1999. The range of dissolved 
oxygen level which was 5.6 to 8.4 in 1986 has risen to 7.1 to 9.0 in 1999. However, 
there has been only an incidental reduction in the level of microbial pollution of the 
treated sewage reaching the river. A total of 835 million litre per day of sewage has 
been intercepted for treatment under the Ganga Action Plan Phase I upto 2000. With 
the completion of the Ganga Action Plan Phase I, only about 35% of the pollution 
generated from towns located along the Ganga has been tackled. The remaining 
pollution is to be tackled under the Ganga Action Plan Phase II which is already under 
70 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
execution. Under this phase, interception and treatment of 1861 million litre per day of 
sewage is proposed. 
(c) While the Ganga Action Plan Phase I has been declared closed since 
31.3.2000, the Ganga Action Plan Phase II is likely to be completed by 2005.

Arbitrary procurement of medicines without ascertaining the requirement from

seven CGHS dispensaries in Pune by placing an indent on GMSD3 Mumbai. The quantity 
of medicines for purchase from GMSD is to be worked out on the basis of requirement 
projected by the seven CGHS dispensaries.

Director during April, 1996 to December, 1997 procured medicines worth Rs. 73.47 
lakh and Rs. 1.53 crore during 1996-97 and 1997-98 respectively from GMSD, 
Mumbai without ascertaining the requirement from the user dispensaries.

during 1996-98, 35 items valued at Rs. 48.40 lakh became time expired as of June

being any demand from the user dispensaries Besides, the Additional Director CGHS 
Pune had to divert medicines valued at Rs. 14.51 lakh to CGHS dispensaries at other 
locations and a Government Hospital to avoid their time expiry.

A Central Bill, titled the Constitution Seventy-Ninth (Amendment) Bill, 1992 
was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on December, 1992. The Bill seeks to amend the 
Directive Principles of State Policy to provide that the State shall endeavour to 
promote population control and the small family norm and to include in the 
Fundamental Duties, a duty to promote and adopt the small family norm. It is also 
proposed that a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a 
member of either House of Parliament or eith er House of Legislature of a State, if he 
has more than two children. 
While recommending the Bill for passage, the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Human Resource Development also recommended that the 
Government may convene a meeting of leaders of various political parties in 
Parliament to ensure the smooth passage of the Bill. 
Accordingly, meet ings of the political parties were held under the 
chairpersonship of MOS(H and FW) on 14th August, 1997 and in December 1999, to 
evolve a consensus for its smooth passage in the Parliament. However, so far, there is no 
consensus among the major political parties, on the subject.

†3493. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: 
SHRI BALKAVI BAIRAGI: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
 whether the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare had issued a notification 
in the Gazette of India on 11 th October, 1999 for use of animal raw material in the tea-
flavour; 
 if so, the names of persons responsible for the same; and 
 what amendments were made in that notification and when? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) to (c) Prior to the 
notification of an amendment to the Preven tion of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules on 
11.10.99, under entries A. Hand A. 14.01 of Appendix B of the PFA 
†Original  notice of the question  was  received  in  Hindi. 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
Rules, 1955, only certain flavours were permissible for producing flavoured tea. There 
was a demand from the tea industry that, with the increasing variety of niche products in 
the market, there was a need to give more flexibility as to the types of flavours which 
may be added to tea. As a result, a notification was issued on 11.10.99, after obtaining 
the recommendations of the Central Committee for Food Standards, deleting the 
limited list of specific flavours permissible for tea. This, in result, made tea subject to 
the general provision for flavours under Rule 63 of the PFA Rules, which applies to all 
items for which there are no specific provis ions. Under Rule 63 of the PFA Rules, the 
products may be flavoured with substances of vegetable or animal origin. 
Since 9.8.94, the PFA Rules, 1955 have included a provision under Rule 44(G) 
under which, inter-alia flavoured tea can only be sold by those manufacturers who are 
registered with the Tea Board. This provision has never been lifted since its inclusion in 
the Rules. Therefore, even after the amendment to entry A. 14 to Appendix B in respect of 
permissible flavours for tea, permission from the Tea Board for adding flavours, was 
necessary before introducing any new flavour for tea. It has been confirmed by the 
competent authorities in the Tea Board that no tea manufacturing company has asked 
for permission for adding flavours containing ingredients of animal origin and no such 
permission has been given by them. 
However, to forestall any misinterpretation of the existing provisions, under 
notification dated 2.08.2000, items A.14 and A.14.01 of Appendix B of the PFA Rules 
have been amended to make it explicit that the flavouring substances permissible in tea 
will be exclusively of materials of vegetable origin. 
The amendments to the PFA Rules including the one made on 11-10-1999 are 
made following the statutory process prescribed for this purpose, which includes 
consultation with the Central Committee for Food Standards (CCFS) comprising 
representatives from State Governments, experts, represen-tatives from other related 
departments of Government etc. vetting by the Ministry of Law and prepublication of 
the draft notification when comments/ objections from the public are invited and 
considered before the final notification is published.

Distortions in Text books 
3508. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that text books prescribed for educational Institutes in 
certain States in the country continue to contain distortions making the impressionable 
minds of students biased against the minority communities; 
 if so, how continuance of such biased school text books can create healthy 
atmosphere and cordial relationship among various communities and sections of 
society in a secular and democratic country; and 
 what measures are contemplated by Government in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) The Nation al Policy on Education envisages a 
National System of Education based on a National Curricular Framework containing a 
common core cutting across different subject areas. Based on the framework 
guidelines and the revised textbooks of the NCERT, the State Governments are 
expected to adopt or adapt, the same for revision of school curricula, syllabi and 
textbooks in their respective school systems in a phased manner. An overwhelming 
majority of the schools in the country are under the control of State Governments and 
they enjoy full autonomy in all school education matters, including prescription of 
syllabi and textbooks within their respective jurisdiction. Whenever any objectionable 
references are brought to the notice of the Union Government, the matter is referred to 
the States for necessary action. The Central Government or its organisations do not have 
any direct role in this matter.

MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) The major recommendations made by Rastogi Committee 
regarding revision of pay scales and service conditions of teachers in universities and 
colleges are as follows: 
 Good academic record, 55% at the Master's level and qualifying the NET 
or an accredited test should be the minimum qualification for the 
appointment of lecturers. 
 The probation should normally be for a period of 24 months, extendable 
upto a further period of 12 months in case of unsatisfactory performance. 
 Posts of professors be provided in the postgraduate colleges. 
 There is need for introducing the concept of pre-induction training 
programmes for the teachers through academic staff colleges. 
 For placement in the senior scale, a lecturer may offer himself/ herself 
for review after 4 years in holding a Ph. D. degree and 6 years if holding 
an M. Phil degree and 7 years if not holding M.Phil/ Ph.D. 
 A Lecturer (Scale) can offer himself/herself for review after 6 years of 
experience as Senior Lecturer, for placement in the Selection Grade. 
 The Merit Promotion Scheme, having dual emoluments or, for the matter, 
any such scheme be dispensed with. 
The Universities/Colleges must observe 180 actual teaching days. 
UGC guidelines regarding minimum number of actual teaching days, 
programme of examination reform and workload for teachers in the 
Universities and Colleges issued in 1989 prescribed that the workload of a 
teacher in full employment should not be less than 40 hours a week for 30 
working weeks in an academic year, which should be ensured. 
The practice of appointing part-time teachers should be sparingly used 
and the remuneration given for such work must be based on realistic 
norms.

3529. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN

dismal, as a recent study has revealed that only 38.5 per cent of primary schools have 
no black boards and about 56 per cent have no pucca buildings; and 
 if so, by when elementary education facilities would be available to all the 
eligible children in the country, by augmenting State Government resources in this 
direction? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) The Central Government supplements the efforts of the 
State Governments and Union Territories Admi nistrations in strengthening elementary 
education infrastructure through Centrally Sponsored Schemes/Programmes such as 
Operation Blackboard and District Primary Education Programme (DPEP). 
168 

[25 August, 2000] R AJYA SABHA 
As per sixth All India Educational Survey (1993) 83.73% primary schools and 
89.30% upper primary schools had pucca and partly pucca buildings. 
However,'34.60% primary sections were found to be deficient in black boards. 
Under the Scheme of Operation Blackboard (OB), 1.82 lakhs classrooms have 
been constructed and financial assistan ce for Teaching Learning Equipment (TLE) 
including black boards has been provided to 5,22,902 primary schools and to 127,257 
upper primary schools. 
District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) is currently in operation in 219 
districts in 15 States. It provides for improvement of physical infrastructure facilities 
and manpower resources in primary school. Under this programme 8,000 formal

Appeal Rules and punishment imposed upon them. To prevent train accidents,

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
following steps are being taken for improvement of staff functioning and equipment 
reliability. 
(i) The work of track circuiting has been accelerated on the trunk routes 
and other important main lines. Fouling Mark to Fouling Mark track 
circuiting work has been completed on A, B, C, D Spl. and D routes. 
(ii) Modification of the signalling circuitry is being carried out to minimise 
chances of human error in causing accidents. 
(iii) Auxiliary Warning System for givi ng advance warning about 'Signal at 
danger' to the driver of the running train has been commissioned on 
Mumbai suburban sections. 
(iv) There has been progressive increase in use of Tie Tamping and ballast 
cleaning machines for track maintenance. 
(v) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of the track, 
sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and portable 
accelerometers are being progressively used. 
(vi) Maintenance facilities for coaches and wagons have been modernised 
and upgraded at many depots. 
(vii) To prevent cases of cold breakage of axles, routine over hauling depots 
have been equipped with ultrasonic testing equipment for detection of 
flaws in the axles. 
(viii) Whistle boards/speed breakers and road signs have been provided at 
unmanned level crossings and visibility for drivers has been improved. 
(ix) Audio-visual publicity campaigns to educate road users on how to make 
a safe crossing are conducted. 
(x) Steps have been taken to prevent inflammable and explosive materials 
from being carried in passenger trains. 
(xi) Training facilities for drivers, guards and staff connected with train 
operation have been modernised including use of Simulators for 
training of drivers. 
(xii)   Refresher courses are regularly organised at specified intervals.

Transgenic crops 
†3559. SHRI RAJIV RANJAN SINGH: SHRI 
RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: 
Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
 whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news item published 
in 'The Times of India' dated 21st July, 2000 under the caption, "concern over effects 
of transgenic crops"; 
 if so, whether it is a fact that many scientific institutions of certain developed 
and developing countries have expressed concern over transgenic food crops; and 
 if so, Government's reaction in this regard?  
†Original  notice of the question  was  received  in  Hindi. 
194 

[25 August, 2000] RA JYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI 
SINGH RAWAT): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The Science Academies around the world including U.K., U.S., 
Brazil, China, Mexico, India and Third World Academy of Sciences have discussed 
various aspects of Transgenic Plants and World Agriculture. Their views are that for 
improving food production and for reducing environmental impacts, a proper 
responsible utilization of scientific discoveries and new technologies are necessary. 
Food can be produced through the use of Genetically Modified technology that are more 
nutritious, stable in storage and in principle, health promoting and bringing benefits to 
consumers in both developing and industrialised nations. Co-operative efforts between 
private and public sectors are needful to develop new transgenic crops that benefit 
consumers, especially in the developing world. Public health regulatory systems need to 
be in place for monitoring the impacts of transgenics. The Academies have welcomed 
Genetically Modified crop technology and have recommended that the technology be 
adopted both by the developed and the developing countries with adequate biosafety 
regulations. The report of the Scientific Academies is a balanced publication. Biosafety 
Guidelines in India are exhaustive and adequate to assess the risks, if any, from the use 
of GM crops to the environment including human and animal health. GM crops can be 
introduced into commercial agriculture only after assessing their safety and agronomic 
advantages.

Operations for Meteorology 
3561. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
 the details of operational services provided by the Ministry in the field of 
Meteorology and surveys through the IMD, SOI and NATMO; 
 the steps taken or proposed to be taken to report and forecast weather 
conditions of each district, especially coasta l districts, through the electronic media of 
each State and the State Governments; and 
 the manner in which the services referred to in parts (a) and (b) above have 
been modernised and how do they compare with similar services in other developed 
countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI 
SINGH RAWAT): (a) India Meteorological Department (IMD) is the principal 
Government Agency in all matters related to meteorology and allied fields in the 
country. IMD's operational responsibilities are: 
 To operate and maintain a network of meteorological observatories. 
 To operate and maintain a telecommunication network for collection and 
dissemination of meteorological data within and outside the country. 
 To issue weather forecasts for the public and users in specific sectors such as 
agriculture, aviation, shipping, fisheries, off-shore oil exploration, etc. 
 To issue warnings against natural disasters like Tropical Cyclones and to 
assist other Disaster Management Agencies including Flood Forecasting. 
 To archive climate data and supply past data to users. 
196 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Survey of India (SOI) is the principal mapping agency of this country and it is 
responsible for ensuring that the country's domain is explored and mapped suitably to 
provide base maps for expeditious and integrated development. SOI provides the 
following services:— 
 To produce all purpose topographical maps required for defence, general 
administration, internal security, developmental needs, irrigation and 
different types of engineering projects. 
 To produce other maps viz. District  Planning Map Series, Tourist Maps, 
Trekking Maps and small scale geographical maps. 
 To carry out project surveys on larger scales according to the 
specifications of the development projects. 
 To provide an accurate positional framework for all significant points on 
earth's surface, especially in and around India. 
 To make use of low altitude remotely sense imageries for topographical 
interpretation and mapping. 
In addition SOI provides the following services in the field of meteorology:— 
 Tidal data on East and West coast, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and 
Lakshadweep Islands is being collected through a network of tidal 
observatories for prediction of tides about one year in advance for the 
purpose of navigational activities and study of variation in mean sea-level. 
 The mapping on 1:25,000 scale with half metre contour interval under 
Coastal Mapping Programme on the East Coast (Nellore to Bangladesh 
Border) in order to study the effect of submergence due to rise in sea-
level and other natural phenomena i.e. Storm surges, cyclones etc. has 
been completed. 
The National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organization (NATMO) provides 
the following services:— 
 To compile the National Atlas of India in English and Hindi. 
 To prepare National Atlas Maps in regional languages. 
 To prepare Thematic Maps based on research studies on 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [25 August, 2000] 
environmental and associated aspects and their impact on social and 
economic development. 
NATMO does not provide any operational services in the field of Meteorology. 
However, in the District Planning Maps, there is an inset depicting the climatic conditions 
of the concerned district. 
In addition to the above, the National Centre for Medium Range Weather 
Forecasting (NCMRWF), New Delhi is providing medium range weather forecast (3—4 
days in advance) based Agrometeorological Advisory Service (AAS) to the farmers 
through 81 AAS units located all over the country. 
 A proven and reliable system for dissemination of district-wise weather 
information and cyclone warnings is already in operation in coastal districts. Under the 
INSAT based Cyclone Warning Dissemination System (CWDS), a total of 250 receiver 
sets have been installed in various coastal districts. The information is disseminated to 
State and Central Government Agencies and to the public through All India Radio and 
Doordarshan, in addition to use of fax/ telephone, high priority telegrams, teleprinter and 
telex messages, police wireless and Newspapers. Farmers' Weather Bulletins are issued 
daily and broadcast from AIR Stations. These bulletins contain district wise weather 
forecasts for next 48 hours with outlook for subsequent two days. IMD issues bi-
weekly agro-meteorological advisories from 17 centres located in state capitals. These 
include district-wise information and are broadcast from AIR stations and also telecast 
from Doordarshan Kendras. In addition there are special programmes arranged on AIR 
and Doordarshan for promoting use of weather information in various agricultural 
practices. 
 State-of-art technology such as Satellite, Radar and Computer Systems is being 
used for weather observation, data exchange, data processing and weather forecasting. 
The INSAT system has been fully exploited for meteorological analysis and weather 
forecasting. A system of 10 S-band conventional radars covers both east and west coasts 
of the country and provides powerful surveillance for detection of tropical cyclones. 
Regional Telecommunication Hub (RTH) under World Meteorological Organization 
has been upgraded to enhance the speed and quantum of data reception and exchange. 
IMD has launched its own internet website (http;//www.imd.emet.in) for dissemination of 
weather information, weather charts and satellite images. Regional Websites have also 
been set up by IMD at Calcutta, Chennai and Mumbai. The forecasts at NCMRWF are 
prepared using a high speed Super

STATEMENT-I 
Salient Features of the Scheme 
1.      Applicability of the Scheme: 
Scheme is for implementation by Commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks 
and Cooperative banks (District Central Cooperative Banks/Primary 
212 

[25 August, 2000] R AJYA SABHA 
Agriculture Cooperative Societies). Implementing banks have the discretion to adopt 
the same to suit location specific requirements. 
2. Objective: 
Kisan Credit Card Scheme aims at adequate and timely support from the banking 
system to the farmers for their cultivation needs including purchase of all inputs in a 
flexible and cost effective manner. 
3. Eligibility: 
The scheme would primarily cater to the short term credit requirements of the 
farmers. Under the scheme, banks may provide the Kisan Credit Cards to farmers who 
are eligible for sanction of production credit. There is no upper and lower limit. 
4. Issue of cards: 
The beneficiaries under the scheme will be issued credit card and pass books or 
credit card-cum- passbooks, incorporating the name, address, particulars of land 
holding, borrowing limit, validity period, etc. which will serve both as an identity card 
as well as facilitate recording of transactions on an on-going basis. 
5. Fixation of credit limit: 
The credit extended under the Kisan Credit Card Scheme is in the nature of 
revolving cash credit and provide for any number of drawals and repayments within the 
limit. While fixing the limits, the entire credit requirements of the farmers for the full 
year are to be taken into account. The credit limit under the card is to be fixed on the 
basis of the operational land holding, cropping pattern and scale of finance as 
recommended by District Level/State Level Committee. 
6. Validity/renewal: 
The validity of the credit card normally should be for a period of 3 years subject 
to an annual review. 
7. Rate of interest: 
Rates of interest are to be charged as applicable to crop loans.

Security/margin norms should be in conformity with the instructions issued by

Launching of PMGY 
*425. CHAUDHARY CHUNNI LAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
 whether a new "Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana" has been launched 
recently; 
 if so, the salient features thereof; 
 the criteria fixed for disbursement of funds to the States under the Scheme; 
and 
 the allocation made during the current year State-wise and the results achieved 
during the last three months? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING AND 
MINISTER OF STATE OF MINISTRY  OF STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME 
IMPLEMENTATION AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF 
ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY 
OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS AND MINISTER OF 
STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) In order to achieve the objective of sustainable human development at the 
village level, Pradhan Mantri  Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) has been launched in the 
Annual Plan 2000-01 in all the States and UTs. 
PMGY envisages allocation of Additional Central Assistance (ACA) to the 
States and UTs for selected basic minimum services. The allocation for PMGY in the 
current year is Rs. 5000 crore. PMGY has two components, namely, rural roads and other 
programmes of PMGY. While the rural roads programme has been allocated Rs. 2500 
crore, the other Programmes of PMGY have also been allocated an equal amount of Rs. 
2500 crore. The rural roads component 
216 

[25 August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of the PMGY is being coordinated by the Department of Rural Development. For the 
other sectoral programmes of PMGY, the concerned Central Administrative 
Departments of Elementary Education and Literacy, Family Welfare, Drinking Water, 
Rural Development and Women and Child Development are responsible for 
coordination and supervision. These Departments have issued guidelines for 
implementation of their sectoral programmes by the State Governments under PMGY. 
As per the guidelines, a minimum of 15 per cent of the ACA allocation of a State must 
be allocated to each of the five sectors under other programmes of PMGY. While 75 per 
cent of the ACA allocation of a State will be spent on the five sectors, the allocation of 
the residual 25 per cent of the ACA will be decided by the States and UTs themselves 
as per their own priorities. 
While the other programmes of PMGY would also be monitored by these Central 
Departments, the overall monitoring of the PMGY would be undertaken by the Planning 
Commission. 
(c) In so far as Special Category States are concerned, approximately 30 
per cent of the total allocation under the other programmes of PMGY has been 
kept aside and distributed among these States on the basis of their proportionate 
share as worked out for the devolution of the normal Central Assistance. 
The relative gaps in the basic services infrastructure/indicator among the States 
have been taken as the criteria for disbursement of the remaining 70 per cent of funds 
among the Non-Special Category States under PMGY. The four sectors which have 
been taken to calculate a State-specific composite weighted average index are Drinking 
Water, Primary Health, Primary Education and Shelter. Each of the four sectors has 
been given equal weightage. As per this criteria, the States which rank low stand to gain 
by a relatively higher allocation of ACA for PMGY. 
The allocation for the rural roads component of PMGY is yet to be finalised by the 
Department of Rural Development. 
(d) The State-wise allocation of ACA made for the current year for the 
other programmes of PMGY is given in the Statement. The first six monthly 
instalments of ACA for all the five sectors to all States and UTs have been 
released during June-July, 2000.

Signing of NPT 
*434. SHRI KARA. SUBBIAN: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that only four nations—Cuba, Israel, Pakistan and India 
have not signed Nuclear Non-proliferation Treaty (NPT); 
 if so, whether it will have any negative effect on India; 
 what is the outcome of the month-long NPT Review Conference; and 
 whether UN Security Council or the NPT Conference exerted pressure on 
India to become a member of the NPT? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH) (a) Yes, 
Sir. 
 This is India's considered and consistent position. 
 The 6th Review Conference of the NPT held in New York from 24th 
April—20th May concluded with the adoption a final document. Although the document 
has a reference to an "unequivocal undertaking" on nuclear disarmament and some 
practical steps to further nuclear disarmament under Article VI of the treaty, there is, 
however, no substantive change in the position of the NPT nuclear weapon States on 
nuclear disarmament. 
 The final document of the NPT Review Conference recalls UN Security Council 
resolution 1172 and calls on India to undertake the measures set out in that resolution 
and to accede to the NPT as a non-nuclear weapon State. India has rejected UN 
Security Council resolution 1172 and maintains that the NPT Community needs to come 
to terms with the realty that India is a nuclear weapon State.
